board_events.text: $\alpha$ = semi-vertical angle (axis to generator), fixed for a cone. $\beta$ = angle the cutting plane makes with the axis.
$\beta = 90^\circ$ gives a circle. $\alpha < \beta < 90^\circ$ gives an ellipse.
$\beta = \alpha$ (plane parallel to a generator) gives a parabola.
$0 \le \beta < \alpha$ gives a hyperbola: the plane cuts BOTH nappes.
Two branches = one plane slicing both cones. That is the hyperbola.
One number tunes the whole family: eccentricity e
A conic = all points whose (distance to focus) divided by (distance to directrix) equals a constant $e$.

board_events.text: $e = 0$: circle. $0 < e < 1$: ellipse.
$e = 1$: parabola. $e > 1$: hyperbola.
Parabola is the hinge: $e = 1$, exactly matching $\beta = \alpha$.
Degenerate case: if the plane passes through the VERTEX, the slice collapses.
Through the vertex you get a single point, one straight line, or a pair of intersecting lines.
Two five-second classifiers
From geometry: compare $\beta$ with $\alpha$, and first check whether the plane hits the vertex.
From an equation with NO $xy$ term: read the signs of $A$ (coeff of $x^2$) and $C$ (coeff of $y^2$).
$A = C$: circle. Same sign but unequal: ellipse. One of them zero: parabola. Opposite signs: hyperbola.
Same sign closes the curve; opposite signs open it into arms.
With an $xy$ term present the conic is rotated, so use the discriminant instead.
$\Delta < 0$: ellipse. $\Delta = 0$: parabola. $\Delta > 0$: hyperbola. Rotation never changes $\Delta$.
Reference: classify by angle, by e, and by equation
By cutting angle (plane not through the vertex):
$\beta = 90^\circ$ circle; $\alpha < \beta < 90^\circ$ ellipse; $\beta = \alpha$ parabola; $0 \le \beta < \alpha$ hyperbola.
By eccentricity: $e = 0$ circle; $0 < e < 1$ ellipse; $e = 1$ parabola; $e > 1$ hyperbola.

segments.text: <curious>Here is the single most useful idea in this whole chapter, so let me say it up front.
The circle, parabola, ellipse and hyperbola are not four unrelated curves to memorise separately. They are one family, four different slices of the same double cone.
Picture two ice-cream cones joined tip to tip, running up and down forever. The meeting point is the vertex, the central line is the axis, and any line down the slope is a generator.
Two angles decide everything. Alpha is the cone's own semi-vertical angle, fixed for a given cone. Beta is the angle at which your cutting plane meets the axis.
Cut straight across, beta equal to ninety degrees, and the slice is a circle. Tilt gently, so alpha is less than beta which is less than ninety, and it stretches into an ellipse.
Keep tilting until the plane runs exactly parallel to one generator, beta equal to alpha. That knife-edge cut is the parabola.
Tilt past that, beta below alpha, and the plane is now steep enough to reach the second cone as well, and that gives a hyperbola.
<whisper>And that is the real reason a hyperbola comes in two branches: your plane is slicing through both nappes of the double cone at once.
There is a second way to see the same family that needs no cone at all, just one number, the eccentricity.
Fix a point called the focus and a line called the directrix. A conic is every point whose distance to the focus, divided by its distance to the directrix, equals a fixed constant e.
Now treat e like a dial. Turn it up from zero and you sweep smoothly through the entire family.
At e equal to zero the shape is perfectly round, a circle. Between zero and one the focus is winning slightly, and you get an ellipse.
At e exactly one the two distances are perfectly balanced, and that is the parabola. Push e above one and the curve tears open into the two arms of a hyperbola.
Notice the parabola sits right on the boundary, e equal to one, the same knife-edge we saw geometrically when beta equalled alpha. Two languages, one fact.
One warning before we move on. Everything so far assumes the cutting plane misses the vertex. If it passes through the vertex, the curve collapses.
Then you get a degenerate conic: just a single point, or one straight line, or a pair of intersecting straight lines. Examiners love testing this edge case.
So how do you actually name a conic in the exam hall? Two quick tests cover almost everything.
If the problem is geometric, compare beta with alpha, but first check whether the plane passes through the vertex, because that would make it degenerate.
If instead you are handed an equation with no x-y cross term, just look at A, the coefficient of x squared, and C, the coefficient of y squared.
If A equals C, it is a circle. Same sign but unequal, an ellipse. If one of them is zero, a parabola. Opposite signs, a hyperbola.
The intuition is clean: coefficients with the same sign curve the graph the same way, so it closes up; opposite signs curve it oppositely, so it opens into arms.
The one case that needs more care is when an x-y term is present, which means the conic is rotated relative to the axes.
Then you fall back on a single quantity, the discriminant: B squared minus four A C.
Negative means ellipse, zero means parabola, positive means hyperbola. And crucially, rotating the axes can never change this value, so it classifies correctly no matter the tilt.
Let me lay out the full reference so you have every classifier in one place.
First, classification straight from the geometry, assuming the plane does not pass through the vertex.
Ninety degrees gives a circle; a gentle tilt between alpha and ninety gives an ellipse; exactly alpha gives a parabola; and anything below alpha gives a hyperbola.
Second, the same family read off the eccentricity: zero for a circle, between zero and one for an ellipse, exactly one for a parabola, and above one for a hyperbola.
Third, and most useful for equations, comes the general second-degree equation.
Every conic in the plane is A x squared plus B x y plus C y squared plus D x plus E y plus F equal to zero, with A, B, C not all zero.
The classifier is its discriminant, B squared minus four A C, worth committing to memory.
Negative gives an ellipse, and a circle specifically when A equals C with no x-y term; zero gives a parabola; positive gives a hyperbola.
In Class eleven the cross term is almost always zero, which simply means the conic's axes line up with the coordinate axes.

sections.title: Naming conics: worked examples I & related topics

board_events.text: Example 1 (CBSE): a cone cut at an angle
Cone with $\alpha = 30^\circ$; plane at $\beta = 50^\circ$, not through the vertex. Name the section.
Compare: $30^\circ < 50^\circ < 90^\circ$, so $\alpha < \beta < 90^\circ$, giving an ELLIPSE.
If instead $\beta = 30^\circ = \alpha$, the plane is parallel to a generator: a PARABOLA.
Example 2 (JEE Main): classify by inspection
No $xy$ term, and the coeffs of $x^2$ and $y^2$ are equal ($A = C = 3$).
Equal squared-term coefficients with no $xy$ term: it is a CIRCLE. No centre or radius needed.
Example 3 (JEE Main): opposite signs
No $xy$ term. $A = 4$ and $C = -9$ have opposite signs.
Positive discriminant, so a HYPERBOLA, hence $e > 1$. The two tests agree.
Example 4 (JEE Advanced): a rotated conic
Negative, so an ELLIPSE. The $xy$ term only rotates it; $\Delta$ is rotation-invariant.
Traps that cost marks
A plane through the vertex is NEVER a normal curve. It is degenerate.
The parabola is a single boundary, not a range: $\beta = \alpha$ and $e = 1$.
A circle needs $A = C$ AND $B = 0$. Equal $x^2,y^2$ coeffs WITH an $xy$ term is a rotated ellipse.
Never rotate axes before classifying; $B^2 - 4AC$ already names the curve.
The two-classifier reflex
Geometry: compare $\beta$ to $\alpha$, and check the vertex first.
Equation: no $xy$ term, read signs of $A$ and $C$; with an $xy$ term, sign of $B^2 - 4AC$.
A circle: all points at a fixed distance from a centre
Tie a goat to a peg with a taut rope; the path it traces is a circle of radius $r$.

board_events.text: In the conic family the circle is the calmest member: eccentricity $e = 0$.
A circle is the limiting ellipse whose two foci have merged into the centre.
Standard form wears its centre and radius openly.
General form hides them inside a quadratic; recover them by completing the square.
Same circle, two costumes: recognising that is most of this topic.

segments.text: Let us put the classifiers to work. Example one is a CBSE-style geometry question.
A cone has semi-vertical angle thirty degrees, and a plane cuts it at fifty degrees to the axis without passing through the vertex. Name the section.
Just compare the angles. Thirty is less than fifty is less than ninety, so alpha is less than beta which is less than ninety, and that is exactly the ellipse condition.
And the follow-up: if the plane were at thirty degrees, equal to alpha, it would run parallel to a generator, giving a parabola, the boundary case.
Example two is a JEE Main speed question, and the whole trick is to not compute anything you do not need.
The equation is three x squared plus three y squared minus twelve x plus six y minus four equals zero.
Look only at the top: there is no x-y term, and the coefficients of x squared and y squared are both three, so A equals C.
Equal squared coefficients with no cross term is the circle signature. It is a circle, and you never had to find the centre or radius to say so.
Example three, JEE Main, shows opposite-sign coefficients.
The equation is four x squared minus nine y squared plus eight x plus thirty-six y minus sixty-eight equals zero.
There is no x-y term, and now A is four while C is minus nine, opposite signs.
Feed that into the discriminant: B squared minus four A C is zero minus four times four times minus nine, which is a hundred and forty-four, positive.

segments.text: Let me derive both equations, because the derivation is itself a favourite board question.
Take the centre at h, k and any point P at x, y on the circle. The defining condition is simply that the distance C P equals the radius r.
Write that distance with the distance formula: the square root of x minus h squared plus y minus k squared equals r.

Both sides are non-negative, so squaring is safe and introduces no false points. That gives the standard equation, x minus h squared plus y minus k squared equals r squared. The whole derivation is just the distance formula with the distance pinned to r.
Now the general form. Start from x squared plus y squared plus two g x plus two f y plus c equals zero, and complete the square on the x-terms and the y-terms separately.
That is the general form as given, and it hides the centre and radius inside.
Completing the square turns it into x plus g squared plus y plus f squared equals g squared plus f squared minus c.

Match this against the standard form and you read off the centre as minus g, minus f, and r squared as g squared plus f squared minus c. Now it is visible why the radius can fail: that expression must be positive.

One more result: if A B is a diameter and P is any other point on the circle, the angle at P is a right angle, the angle in a semicircle. Writing perpendicular slopes and clearing fractions gives the diameter form directly.
Example one, CBSE, asks for the centre and radius from a general-form circle.
The circle is x squared plus y squared minus six x plus eight y minus eleven equals zero.
Match against the general form: two g is minus six, so g is minus three; two f is eight, so f is four; and c is minus eleven.
The centre is minus g, minus f, which is three, minus four. The radius is the square root of g squared plus f squared minus c, that is nine plus sixteen plus eleven, thirty-six, whose root is six.
Example two, JEE Main, hands you the two ends of a diameter, so reach straight for the diameter form.
The ends are A at one, two and B at five, six.
The diameter form is x minus one times x minus five, plus y minus two times y minus six, all equal to zero.
Expand and tidy up and you get x squared plus y squared minus six x minus eight y plus seventeen equals zero. One line of setup instead of three.
Example three, JEE Main, chains three ideas: radius as a distance, the equation, and the position test.
The circle has centre two, minus one and passes through the point five, three.
The radius is just the distance from the centre to that point: root of three squared plus four squared, which is root twenty-five, five.
So the equation is x minus two squared plus y plus one squared equals twenty-five.
Now test the point four, two using S-one. Plugging in gives sixteen plus four minus sixteen plus four minus twenty, which is minus twelve, negative, so the point lies inside the circle.
Example four is Advanced: find the circle through three points, then a tangent length.
Substitute the three points O, A and B into the general form. The origin gives c equal to zero; the point six, zero gives g equal to minus three; the point zero, eight gives f equal to minus four.

So the circle is x squared plus y squared minus six x minus eight y equals zero, with centre three, four and radius five. A neat check: O A and O B are perpendicular, so A B is a diameter, and its midpoint three, four is indeed the centre.
For the tangent from the point seven, nine, compute S-one: forty-nine plus eighty-one minus forty-two minus seventy-two, which is sixteen. The tangent length is its square root, four units.
Let me close the circle with the mistakes that quietly drain marks.
The biggest is the centre sign. From the general form the centre is minus g, minus f. Halve the linear coefficients and flip the sign. It is never plain g, f, and never twice that.
Second, always confirm that g squared plus f squared minus c is positive before announcing a radius. Zero gives only a point circle, and negative gives no real circle.
Third, if a problem gives you the two ends of a diameter, the one-line diameter form is faster and safer than computing the centre and radius separately.
Fourth, a real circle must have equal x-squared and y-squared coefficients and no x-y term. If those coefficients differ, you are not even looking at a circle.
Here is the reflex that ties it together, done in a single pass over the equation.
Read g as half the x-coefficient and f as half the y-coefficient; then the centre is minus g, minus f and the radius is the root of g squared plus f squared minus c.
And remember S-one does double duty: plug a point into the circle's left side, its sign tells you out, on, or in, and its square root is the tangent length.

sections.title: The parabola: mirror of one focus & related topics

board_events.text: Parabola: equidistant from a focus and a directrix
A parabola is every point equally far from a fixed point (focus) and a fixed line (directrix).
That balance is exactly eccentricity $e = 1$: (distance to focus) = (distance to directrix).
Focus and directrix are the two ingredients; the vertex sits midway between them.
Rays parallel to the axis all reflect through the focus.
This is why headlights, dish antennas and solar cookers are parabolic.
One axis of symmetry runs through focus and vertex, perpendicular to the directrix.
Unlike ellipse or hyperbola, a parabola has ONE focus and ONE directrix.
Set up: focus $(a,0)$, directrix $x = -a$, vertex at the origin
Let $P(x,y)$ lie on the parabola. Distance to focus = distance to directrix.
Vertex $(0,0)$; focus $(a,0)$; directrix $x = -a$; axis is the x-axis.

segments.text: <curious>The parabola is the conic with a split personality: one focus, one directrix, perfectly balanced between them.
Formally, a parabola is the set of all points that are exactly as far from a fixed point, the focus, as they are from a fixed line, the directrix.
That perfect balance is precisely eccentricity equal to one: the distance to the focus always equals the distance to the directrix, never more, never less.
The two ingredients are the focus and the directrix, and the vertex is simply the midpoint between them, the closest the curve comes to either.
Here is the property that makes the parabola an engineer's favourite: every ray coming in parallel to the axis reflects off the curve and passes through the focus.
Reverse it and a source at the focus sends out a parallel beam. That single fact is why headlights, dish antennas, and solar cookers are all parabolic.
The whole shape is symmetric about one line, the axis, which runs through the focus and vertex and meets the directrix at a right angle.
And note the contrast with what is coming: an ellipse and a hyperbola each have two foci, but a parabola has just one focus and one directrix.

Let me derive the standard parabola so the formula never feels arbitrary. Place the focus at a, zero and the directrix as the vertical line x equals minus a, with the vertex at the origin exactly halfway between.
Take any point P at x, y on the curve. The defining rule says its distance to the focus equals its distance to the directrix.
Distance to the focus is the root of x minus a squared plus y squared. Distance to the vertical directrix is simply x plus a. Set them equal.
Square both sides, which is safe since both are non-negative, and you get x minus a squared plus y squared equals x plus a squared.
Expand, the x squared and a squared terms cancel, the cross terms combine, and everything collapses to the clean standard form, y squared equals four a x.
Read the geometry straight off: the vertex is the origin, the focus is a, zero, the directrix is x equals minus a, and the axis is the x-axis itself.
Here is the full picture: vertex at the tip, focus inside the curve, directrix the same distance out on the other side, and the latus rectum as the chord through the focus.
That latus rectum, the focal chord perpendicular to the axis, always has length four a. It is the quickest measure of how wide the parabola is.
And a itself is the focal distance from the vertex; a larger a pushes the focus out and opens the parabola wider.
There are four standard parabolas, but you never memorise four separate things. One rule reads all of them.
Look at the grid: right-opening, left-opening, up-opening, down-opening, each with its own equation.
y squared equals four a x opens to the right, toward positive x; put a minus sign, y squared equals minus four a x, and it opens to the left.
Swap the roles: x squared equals four a y opens upward, and with a minus sign, x squared equals minus four a y, it opens downward.
Here is the rule that generates all four: the variable that is squared tells you the axis, and the sign on the other side tells you which way it opens.
So if y is the squared variable, the axis is the x-axis; if x is squared, the axis is the y-axis. The parabola always opens along the axis of the squared variable.
And the numbers transfer unchanged: the size of four a is always the latus rectum, and the focus always sits a distance a from the vertex along that axis.
One more reading: because there is no linear term in the squared variable, the vertex sits at the origin. Shifted parabolas just move that vertex elsewhere.
Here is the whole parabola toolkit in one board.
The two horizontal-axis parabolas: y squared equals four a x opening right, and y squared equals minus four a x opening left.
The two vertical-axis parabolas: x squared equals four a y opening up, and x squared equals minus four a y opening down.
Let me give every element for the reference case, y squared equals four a x, and you adapt the rest by symmetry.
The focus is a, zero, and the directrix is the line x equals minus a, the same distance on the far side of the vertex.
The vertex is the origin and the axis is the line y equals zero, the x-axis.
The latus rectum has length four a, with its endpoints at a, plus and minus two a, straight above and below the focus.
For the other three forms, simply swap the roles of x and y and flip the sign to match the direction the curve opens.
And the number-one habit: read four a as a single block first. Match your equation to four a, then halve twice to get a. That alone kills most parabola errors.

Example 2 (JEE Main): build the equation from focus and directrix

$x$ is squared (axis is the y-axis), it opens DOWN, and $a = 2$.
Example 3 (JEE Main): equation from vertex and focus
Vertex $(0,0)$, focus $(5,0)$: focus on $+x$-axis, so it opens right, $a = 5$.
Example 4 (JEE Adv): a parabolic reflector
A dish is $20$ cm across and $5$ cm deep. Vertex at origin, opening up: $x^2 = 4ay$.
The rim point $(10, 5)$ lies on the curve (half-width $10$, depth $5$).
The receiver sits at the focus, $5$ cm above the vertex: the reflector property at work.
Parabola traps
Read $4a$ as one block. $y^2 = 12x$ gives $4a = 12$, so $a = 3$, NOT $a = 12$.
The squared variable names the axis; the sign of the other side names the direction.
The focus is INSIDE the curve; the directrix is OUTSIDE, the same distance $a$ from the vertex.
A parabola has ONE focus and ONE directrix, and eccentricity is exactly $1$.

Spot the squared variable and the sign, match $4a$, then place the focus at $a$ and directrix at $-a$.

segments.text: Example one, CBSE, is the bread-and-butter task: read every element off a given parabola.
The equation is y squared equals twelve x.
Match four a to twelve, so a is three. Since y is squared and the right side is positive, the parabola opens to the right.
That immediately gives the focus at three, zero, the directrix x equals minus three, and a latus rectum of twelve. Done, with no calculation beyond one division.
Example two, JEE Main, runs the other way: you are given the focus and directrix and must build the equation.
The focus is zero, minus two and the directrix is the line y equals two. The vertex sits midway between them, which is the origin.
The focus is directly below the vertex, so the axis is the y-axis, x is the squared variable, and the curve opens downward. The focal distance a is two.
So the form is x squared equals minus four a y, with a equal to two, giving x squared equals minus eight y. The minus sign encodes the downward opening.
Example three, JEE Main, gives the vertex and focus and asks for the equation.
The vertex is the origin and the focus is five, zero, sitting on the positive x-axis. So the parabola opens to the right with focal distance a equal to five.
Plug a equals five into y squared equals four a x and you get y squared equals twenty x. Two facts in, one equation out.
Example four is the Advanced application, a real parabolic dish, and it shows why the vertex-at-origin trick is so powerful.
The dish is twenty centimetres across and five centimetres deep. Put the vertex at the origin with the dish opening upward, so the form is x squared equals four a y.
The rim is ten centimetres out on each side and five deep, so the point ten, five lies on the parabola.
Substitute: ten squared is four a times five, that is a hundred equals twenty a, so a equals five.
The dish is x squared equals twenty y, and the focus is at zero, five, five centimetres straight up from the vertex.
That focus is exactly where you mount the receiver, because every incoming parallel signal reflects straight to it. The abstract property becomes a design instruction.
Let me close the parabola with the mistakes that cost the most marks.
The single biggest one: read four a as a single block. In y squared equals twelve x, four a is twelve, so a is three. Students who set a equal to twelve get the focus and directrix wrong every time.
Second, keep the orientation rule straight: the squared variable names the axis, and the sign of the other side names the direction it opens.
Third, do not swap focus and directrix. The focus lies inside the curve; the directrix is a line outside it, the same distance a from the vertex on the opposite side.
Fourth, remember what makes it a parabola at all: exactly one focus, one directrix, and eccentricity precisely one, never a range.
Here is the one-pass reflex for any standard parabola.
Spot which variable is squared and the sign, match the coefficient to four a, then place the focus at distance a and the directrix at minus a along the axis.
And keep the latus-rectum endpoints handy, a, plus and minus two a for y squared equals four a x. Three points and a direction give you a clean sketch in seconds.

sections.title: The ellipse: two pins and a string & related topics

board_events.text: Ellipse: constant total distance to TWO foci
Pin a loop of string over two tacks and trace it taut: the path is an ellipse.
For every point, (distance to $F_1$) + (distance to $F_2$) = constant = $2a$.
The two tacks are the foci; the string length fixes $2a$.
Eccentricity lives strictly between $0$ and $1$: a squashed, closed curve.
As the foci merge, $e \to 0$ and the ellipse becomes a circle.
As the foci spread toward the ends, $e \to 1$ and it grows long and thin.
A circle is just the ellipse with both foci at the centre.
Foci $(\pm c, 0)$, string length $2a$
For $P(x,y)$: $PF_1 + PF_2 = 2a$, with $a > c > 0$.
Isolate one root, square, simplify, then square again.
Here $a$ = semi-major axis, $b$ = semi-minor axis, and $a > b$.
$b^2 = a^2 - c^2$ is the master link: it ties axis lengths to focal distance.
Which axis is major? The larger denominator wins

$a^2$ is ALWAYS the larger denominator; it sits under the major axis's variable.

segments.text: <curious>The ellipse has a beautifully physical definition you can build with two tacks and a loop of string.
Pin the loop over two tacks, pull it taut with a pencil, and drag the pencil all the way round. The closed oval it traces is an ellipse.
Why does that work? For every point on the curve, the sum of the distances to the two fixed points, the foci, stays constant. We call that constant two a.
The two tacks are the foci, and the length of your string fixes two a. Change the string and you change the size and shape.
In eccentricity terms the ellipse lives strictly between zero and one, a closed curve that is a squashed circle.
Push the two foci together and the sum condition forces equal radii in all directions, so e goes to zero and the ellipse becomes a circle.
Pull the foci apart toward the far ends and e climbs toward one, stretching the ellipse long and thin.
So the circle is not separate from the ellipse; it is the special ellipse with both foci sitting on top of each other at the centre.
Let me derive the ellipse, because the derivation hands you the single most useful relationship in the topic. Put the foci at plus and minus c on the x-axis, and let the string length be two a.
For any point P on the curve, the distance to the first focus plus the distance to the second equals two a, and physically the string must reach across, so a is bigger than c.
Written out, that is the root of x plus c squared plus y squared, plus the root of x minus c squared plus y squared, equals two a. Two square roots is awkward, so we clear them in stages.
Move one root to the other side, square once to kill it, simplify, isolate the remaining root, and square a second time. It is algebra-heavy but completely mechanical.
When the dust settles you get x squared over a squared plus y squared over a squared minus c squared equals one.
Now define b squared as a squared minus c squared, and the equation becomes the clean standard form, x squared over a squared plus y squared over b squared equals one.
Here a is the semi-major axis, the longer half-width, and b is the semi-minor axis, the shorter one, so a is greater than b whenever the foci are on the x-axis.
The focal distance c relates to size through c equals a e, so the eccentricity e is c over a, and because c is less than a, e always sits strictly between zero and one.
Commit b squared equals a squared minus c squared to memory. It is the master link tying the two axis lengths to the focal distance, and almost every ellipse problem uses it.
The one decision that trips people is which way the ellipse is oriented, so let me make it mechanical.
Here is a horizontal ellipse fully labelled: the centre, the two vertices at the ends of the long axis, the two foci inside, and the semi-axes a and b.
If the equation is x squared over a squared plus y squared over b squared equals one, with a greater than b, the major axis runs along the x-axis.
If instead a squared sits under y squared, so x squared over b squared plus y squared over a squared, the major axis runs along the y-axis. Nothing else changes.
The rule that decides it: a squared is always the larger denominator, and it sits under the variable of the major axis. Find the bigger denominator and you have found the long direction.
The two vertices are two a apart along the major axis, and the minor axis has total length two b across the short direction.
The foci always lie on the major axis, each a distance c from the centre, where c is the root of a squared minus b squared.
And the directrices are the two lines perpendicular to the major axis at plus and minus a over e, mirroring the focus-directrix idea from the parabola.

board_events.text: Example 1 (CBSE): all elements from the equation
Larger denom $25$ under $x^2$: $a^2 = 25,\ b^2 = 9$, so $a = 5,\ b = 3$; major axis on x.
Example 2 (JEE Main): watch the orientation
Now $25$ is under $y^2$: major axis on y, foci $(0,\pm 4)$, vertices $(0,\pm 5)$.
Example 3 (JEE Main): build from foci and vertices
Vertices $(\pm 6,0)$, foci $(\pm 4,0)$: so $a = 6,\ c = 4$, major axis on x.
Example 4 (JEE Adv): from eccentricity and a length
Foci on x-axis, $e = \tfrac{1}{2}$, major axis length $10$, so $a = 5$.
Half the major axis is $a$; never plug the full length $2a$ into a formula.
Ellipse traps
$a^2$ is the BIGGER denominator. Its variable marks the major axis.
Foci lie on the MAJOR axis, never the minor one; check orientation before placing them.
Use $b^2 = a^2 - c^2$ (subtract); do not mis-remember it as $a^2 = b^2 - c^2$.
In formulas $a,b$ are SEMI-axes; halve any full axis length first.
The identify-first reflex
Step 1: bigger denom is $a^2$, so that variable's axis is major. Step 2: $c = \sqrt{a^2 - b^2}$.
Then $e = c/a$, foci on the major axis, and LR $= 2b^2/a$ all follow.

segments.text: Example one, CBSE, is the standard read-off task.
The ellipse is x squared over twenty-five plus y squared over nine equals one.
The larger denominator, twenty-five, sits under x squared, so a squared is twenty-five and b squared is nine, giving a equals five and b equals three, with the major axis on the x-axis.
Then c is the root of twenty-five minus nine, which is four, and the eccentricity is c over a, four over five, zero point eight.
So the vertices are plus and minus five, zero, the foci plus and minus four, zero, and the latus rectum is two times nine over five, three point six.
Example two, JEE Main, looks almost identical but flips the orientation, and that is the whole point.
Now the ellipse is x squared over nine plus y squared over twenty-five equals one.

This time twenty-five sits under y squared, so the major axis is vertical. The foci move to zero, plus and minus four, and the vertices to zero, plus and minus five. Same numbers, rotated ninety degrees, because the bigger denominator moved.
Example three, JEE Main, gives you the vertices and foci and asks for the equation.
The vertices are plus and minus six, zero and the foci plus and minus four, zero, so a is six, c is four, and the major axis is on the x-axis.
Use the master relation: b squared equals a squared minus c squared, thirty-six minus sixteen, which is twenty.
So the ellipse is x squared over thirty-six plus y squared over twenty equals one. Two points of data straight into one equation.
Example four, Advanced, gives the eccentricity and a length instead, which is a favourite twist.
The foci are on the x-axis, e is one half, and the major axis has length ten. Halve that length to get a equals five, not ten.
Then c is a e, five times one half, two point five; and b squared is a squared minus c squared, twenty-five minus six point two five, eighteen point seven five.
So the ellipse is x squared over twenty-five plus y squared over eighteen point seven five equals one.
And note the trap that snares half the class: the a in every formula is the semi-major axis, half the full length. Plugging in the whole two a instead of a doubles your answer and loses the marks.
Let me close the ellipse with the traps examiners set again and again.
First and biggest: a squared is the larger denominator, and the variable above it marks the major axis. Get this backwards and every element lands in the wrong place.
Second, the foci always sit on the major axis, never the minor one. So decide the orientation before you place a single focus.

Third, use the relation the right way round: b squared equals a squared minus c squared, a subtraction. Students who mangle it into a squared equals b squared minus c squared get negative lengths and panic.
Fourth, in every formula a and b are the semi-axes, the half-lengths. If a question gives you a full axis length, halve it before it touches a formula.
Here is the reflex that keeps you safe.
Step one: the bigger denominator is a squared, and its variable's axis is the major one. Step two: get c from the root of a squared minus b squared.
After that everything cascades: e is c over a, the foci go on the major axis at distance c, and the latus rectum is two b squared over a. Identify first, and the formulas run themselves.

sections.title: The hyperbola: a constant difference & related topics

board_events.text: Hyperbola: constant DIFFERENCE of distances to two foci
For every point, $|PF_1 - PF_2|$ = constant = $2a$. Difference, not sum.
Ellipse adds the two distances; hyperbola subtracts them.
Eccentricity is greater than $1$: the curve is open, with two branches.
Each branch hugs a pair of straight lines called asymptotes but never touches them.
Used in navigation (LORAN), cooling towers, and the orbits of fast comets.
The transverse axis joins the two vertices; the conjugate axis is perpendicular to it.
Foci sit OUTSIDE the vertices: $c > a$, unlike the ellipse where $a > c$.
Foci $(\pm c, 0)$, constant difference $2a$, with $c > a$
Isolate a root, square, simplify, then square again (as for the ellipse).
Same algebra as the ellipse, but $c > a$ flips a sign: PLUS becomes MINUS.
The asymptotes are the hyperbola's skeleton

segments.text: <curious>The hyperbola is the ellipse's mirror twin: swap one word in the definition and the whole shape flips open.
Instead of the sum of the two focal distances, the hyperbola keeps their difference constant. For every point, the absolute difference of the distances to the two foci equals two a.
That one change, subtract instead of add, is the whole story. An ellipse adds and closes; a hyperbola subtracts and opens.
Its eccentricity is always greater than one, and because of that the curve never closes: it breaks into two separate branches facing away from each other.
Each branch runs alongside a pair of straight lines called asymptotes, getting ever closer but never quite touching, like rails vanishing to the horizon.
This shape is everywhere in engineering: the LORAN navigation system, the curved profile of cooling towers, and the paths of comets that swing past the sun once and leave.
The line joining the two vertices is the transverse axis, and the perpendicular one through the centre is the conjugate axis.
And here is the key contrast to hold onto: the foci lie outside the vertices, so c is greater than a. In the ellipse it was the other way round, a greater than c.

Let me derive the hyperbola right after the ellipse, because the algebra is almost identical and the one difference is deeply instructive. Put the foci at plus and minus c, but now c is bigger than a.
The defining condition is that the absolute difference of the two focal distances equals two a.
Written out, the root of x plus c squared plus y squared minus the root of x minus c squared plus y squared equals plus or minus two a, the sign depending on which branch you are on.
The clearing of roots is the same routine as the ellipse: isolate one root, square, simplify, isolate the other, square again. Nothing new to learn.
You land on exactly the same intermediate form as the ellipse: x squared over a squared plus y squared over a squared minus c squared equals one.

But here is where the two conics part ways. For the ellipse c was smaller than a, so a squared minus c squared was positive. For the hyperbola c is bigger than a, so that quantity is negative, and we define b squared as c squared minus a squared, which is now the positive one.
Substituting flips the plus to a minus, giving the standard hyperbola: x squared over a squared minus y squared over b squared equals one.

And the focal relation flips with it: instead of b squared equals a squared minus c squared, we now have c squared equals a squared plus b squared, so c is the largest of the three and the eccentricity c over a is above one.
So do not memorise the hyperbola as a fresh formula. It is the ellipse derivation with c bigger than a, and that single fact turns the plus sign into a minus.
The single most important feature of a hyperbola is its pair of asymptotes, because they are the skeleton the whole curve is draped over.
In the picture, the two dashed diagonals are the asymptotes. Each branch sweeps out from its vertex and presses closer and closer to them without ever meeting.

For x squared over a squared minus y squared over b squared equals one, the asymptotes are simply y equals plus and minus b over a times x. Sketch those two lines first and the branches almost draw themselves.

Now orientation, and this is where the hyperbola differs sharply from the ellipse. The variable with the positive term marks the transverse axis. With x squared positive, the hyperbola opens left and right.
Flip the signs, y squared over a squared minus x squared over b squared equals one, and now the y squared term is positive, so the hyperbola opens up and down instead.
Burn this in: for a hyperbola it is the sign that decides orientation, not the larger denominator. That rule was for the ellipse; do not carry it over.
One special case shows up often: the rectangular or equilateral hyperbola, where a equals b. Then the eccentricity is exactly root two and the two asymptotes meet at right angles.
And the familiar curve x y equals c squared is just that same rectangular hyperbola, rotated so that the coordinate axes themselves are its asymptotes.

You land on exactly the same intermediate form as the ellipse: x squared over a squared plus y squared over a squared minus c squared equals one.

But here is where the two conics part ways. For the ellipse c was smaller than a, so a squared minus c squared was positive. For the hyperbola c is bigger than a, so that quantity is negative, and we define b squared as c squared minus a squared, which is now the positive one.
Substituting flips the plus to a minus, giving the standard hyperbola: x squared over a squared minus y squared over b squared equals one.

And the focal relation flips with it: instead of b squared equals a squared minus c squared, we now have c squared equals a squared plus b squared, so c is the largest of the three and the eccentricity c over a is above one.
So do not memorise the hyperbola as a fresh formula. It is the ellipse derivation with c bigger than a, and that single fact turns the plus sign into a minus.
The single most important feature of a hyperbola is its pair of asymptotes, because they are the skeleton the whole curve is draped over.
In the picture, the two dashed diagonals are the asymptotes. Each branch sweeps out from its vertex and presses closer and closer to them without ever meeting.

For x squared over a squared minus y squared over b squared equals one, the asymptotes are simply y equals plus and minus b over a times x. Sketch those two lines first and the branches almost draw themselves.

Now orientation, and this is where the hyperbola differs sharply from the ellipse. The variable with the positive term marks the transverse axis. With x squared positive, the hyperbola opens left and right.
Flip the signs, y squared over a squared minus x squared over b squared equals one, and now the y squared term is positive, so the hyperbola opens up and down instead.
Burn this in: for a hyperbola it is the sign that decides orientation, not the larger denominator. That rule was for the ellipse; do not carry it over.
One special case shows up often: the rectangular or equilateral hyperbola, where a equals b. Then the eccentricity is exactly root two and the two asymptotes meet at right angles.
And the familiar curve x y equals c squared is just that same rectangular hyperbola, rotated so that the coordinate axes themselves are its asymptotes.

board_events.text: Example 1 (CBSE): all elements from the equation
$x^2$ term positive: opens left-right. $a^2 = 16,\ b^2 = 9$, so $a = 4,\ b = 3$.
Example 2 (JEE Main): a larger denominator under the negative term
$y^2$ positive, so opens UP-DOWN: $a^2 = 9$ (transverse), $b^2 = 25$; note $b > a$ is fine.
Example 3 (JEE Main): build from vertices and foci
Vertices $(\pm 3,0)$, foci $(\pm 5,0)$: so $a = 3,\ c = 5$, opens left-right.
Example 4 (JEE Adv): from eccentricity and latus rectum
$e = 2$ and latus rectum $= 12$, foci on the x-axis.
Hyperbola traps (mostly ellipse habits leaking in)
Sign, not size: the POSITIVE term marks the transverse axis. $b > a$ is allowed.
Use $c^2 = a^2 + b^2$ (add). $c$ is the LARGEST; foci lie outside the vertices.
Eccentricity is always $> 1$; $e = \sqrt{2}$ is the rectangular case ($a = b$).
Always sketch the asymptotes $y = \pm (b/a)x$ first; the branches follow.
Ellipse versus hyperbola at a glance
Ellipse: PLUS sign, $c^2 = a^2 - b^2$, $e < 1$, closed. Hyperbola: MINUS sign, $c^2 = a^2 + b^2$, $e > 1$, open.
Same read-off skills; the sign between the terms flips every conclusion.

segments.text: Example one, CBSE, is the standard element read-off, and the very first thing to check is the sign.
The hyperbola is x squared over sixteen minus y squared over nine equals one.
The x squared term is positive, so it opens left and right. Since the positive term fixes the transverse axis, a squared is sixteen and b squared is nine, giving a equals four and b equals three.
Now use the plus relation: c is the root of sixteen plus nine, which is five, and the eccentricity is c over a, five over four, one point two five, comfortably above one.
So the vertices are plus and minus four, zero, the foci plus and minus five, zero, and the asymptotes are y equals plus and minus three-quarters x.
Example two, JEE Main, is designed to catch the student who imported the ellipse rule. The equation is y squared over nine minus x squared over twenty-five equals one.
Read the sign, not the size. The y squared term is positive, so this hyperbola opens up and down, and a squared is nine, sitting under the transverse variable.

Here b squared is twenty-five, bigger than a squared. For a hyperbola that is perfectly normal, because orientation follows the sign, not which denominator is larger. Do not let a smaller denominator on the positive term fool you.
Example three, JEE Main, hands you the vertices and foci and asks for the equation.
The vertices are plus and minus three, zero and the foci plus and minus five, zero, so a is three, c is five, and the curve opens left and right.
Use the plus relation solved for b: b squared equals c squared minus a squared, twenty-five minus nine, which is sixteen.
So the hyperbola is x squared over nine minus y squared over sixteen equals one. Two data points, one equation.
Example four, Advanced, combines the eccentricity with the latus rectum, so you solve two relations together.
You are told the eccentricity is two and the latus rectum is twelve, with the foci on the x-axis.
From e squared equals one plus b squared over a squared, with e equal to two, b squared over a squared is three. And the latus rectum, two b squared over a, equals twelve.

Substitute b squared equals three a squared into the latus-rectum equation: two times three a squared over a is six a, set equal to twelve, so a is two, and then b squared is three times four, twelve.
So the hyperbola is x squared over four minus y squared over twelve equals one. Two conditions, two unknowns, cleanly solved.
Almost every hyperbola mistake is really an ellipse habit that leaked across, so let me line them up.

First and biggest: sign, not size. The positive term marks the transverse axis, and it is completely fine for b to be bigger than a. Do not pick the axis by the larger denominator; that was the ellipse.
Second, the focal relation adds: c squared equals a squared plus b squared. So c is the largest of the three and the foci sit outside the vertices, the reverse of the ellipse.
Third, the eccentricity is always greater than one, and the neat special value e equals root two is exactly the rectangular case where a equals b.
Fourth, a practical one: always draw the asymptotes y equals plus and minus b over a x before the curve. With the frame in place, each branch almost sketches itself.
Let me put the two conics side by side so the contrast is impossible to forget.

The ellipse has a plus sign, c squared equals a squared minus b squared, eccentricity below one, and it is closed. The hyperbola has a minus sign, c squared equals a squared plus b squared, eccentricity above one, and it is open.
The read-off skills are identical; it is the single sign between the two terms that flips every conclusion, from orientation to the focal relation to the shape.

board_events.text: Every circle formula you need
$g^2 + f^2 - c$: positive = real, zero = point circle, negative = imaginary.
That is the diameter form, with $A(x_1,y_1)$ and $B(x_2,y_2)$ as the diameter ends.
Sign of $S_1$: outside, on, or inside. Tangent length from an outside point is $\sqrt{S_1}$.
Ellipse essentials (major axis on x-axis, $a > b$)
For a vertical major axis, swap $a^2,b^2$ and read the foci as $(0, \pm c)$.
Identify $a^2$ (bigger) and $b^2$ (smaller) FIRST; every formula follows.
Hyperbola essentials (transverse axis on x-axis)
Transverse axis on the y-axis: $\dfrac{y^2}{a^2} - \dfrac{x^2}{b^2} = 1$, foci $(0, \pm c)$.
Ellipse: $c^2 = a^2 - b^2$. Hyperbola: $c^2 = a^2 + b^2$. Only the sign differs.
Your complete conic-sections toolkit
Eccentricity ladder: circle $0$, ellipse $0$ to $1$, parabola $1$, hyperbola $> 1$.

board_events.text: Conic Sections in 60 seconds
Classifier: same sign closes (circle/ellipse), opposite signs open (hyperbola); a missing square means a parabola.
Eccentricity: $0$ circle, $0$ to $1$ ellipse, $1$ parabola, $> 1$ hyperbola.
Circle: centre $(-g,-f)$, $r = \sqrt{g^2+f^2-c}$; $S_1$ sign locates a point, $\sqrt{S_1}$ is the tangent.
Parabola: read $4a$ as a block; the squared variable is the axis, its sign is the opening direction.
Ellipse: bigger denominator is $a^2$; $b^2 = a^2-c^2$; foci on the major axis; LR $= 2b^2/a$.
